p. 40) *Cinmantramālinī*:
Now, the sequence for the worship of the fifteen *Nityās* is set forth—beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the end of the fortnight (*parvan*).

One should perform the recitation during all three junctions (saṃdhyā) by reciting the respective vidyās—beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā—on their corresponding lunar days, repeating them according to the sequence of sixty ghaṭikās. For example:
at the time of the morning bath, having recited the respective vidyā three times and having drunk water, one should [recite] that respective vidyā...

Having recited the mantra, sprinkled oneself with water, and performed the preliminary rites such as changing into three garments and the *saṃdhyā-vandana*, one should sit facing east upon a soft seat in a clean place or in one's own home; then, assuming the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), one should perform *prāṇāyāma*, *bhūtaśuddhi*, and so forth.

Having prepared charcoal scented with camphor, having meditated upon the Guru on one's own head, having gratified and prostrated before him, and having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, [one should say]: "On this first lunar day, desiring to please Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, I shall perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Kāmeśvarī-nityā* mantra. Thus.
Having performed the mental visualization (*saṃkalpa*): *aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *sakalahrīṃ śirase svāhā*;
*nityāśikhāyaivaṣaṭ*; *kinne kavacāya huṃ*; *madradrave netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*; *sauḥ*.

*Phaṭ* to the weapon. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, one should place *aiṃ sakalahrīṃ* on the two eyes; *nitya* on the two ears; *klinna* on the nose; *jihvā* on the tongue; *hṛd* on the heart; *i* on the navel; *ve* on the secret place; and *sauḥ* on all the limbs.
Having thus performed the placement one by one in these locations and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the entire mantra, one should meditate.
Resembling ten million rising suns, radiant with a crown of rubies,
adorned with necklaces, neck-ornaments, girdles, rings, anklets, and other jewels; clothed in red garments and beautified by crimson ornaments.
She has six arms and three eyes, her head is adorned with a digit of the moon,
and she resides within a hexagon, an octagon, a sixteen-petaled lotus, a pair [of triangles], and a square.
Her face shines with a gentle smile, and her gaze is languid with compassion.
Holding in her hands a noose, a goad, a lotus, a sugarcane bow, a flower-arrow,
and a jewel-vessel filled with molasses, and bestowing boons— having meditated thus, having formed the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as intended, once again...

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā. The root mantra is: *aiṃ sakala kahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ*. This is the root mantra of Kāmeśvarī.
On the second day, having performed the morning bath and other rites as before, one should recite the Bhagamālinī-vidyā.

Having performed the salutation to the Guru and the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should assign [the mantras] to the hands and limbs as follows: "Aiṃ, obeisance to the heart; Bhagabhagāvahe, Phaṭ to the weapon. Having thus performed the assignment for the hands and limbs and having performed the pervasive assignment (*vyāpaka*) with the entire mantra, one should meditate upon her: ruddy, appearing as if ruddy, O beautiful one, with a smiling face, three-eyed, and endowed with six arms.
Holding in her right arms a lotus, a lily, a noose, a *puṇḍraka* flower, and a sugarcane stalk, and likewise in her left arms a lotus, a goad, and the arrows of the Flower-Bowed God (Kāmadeva).
Having meditated thus upon her who is praised by hosts of attendants, powers, and Gaṇas on all sides, and having formed the Yonimudrā, one should perform the recitation as intended;
then, having again performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), one should practice the worship of Śrīvidyā. *Aiṃ bhagabhugebhāgeni bhagodare*.

O you who possess the vulva, O bringer of the vulva, O secret of the vulva, O womb of the vulva, O you who strike down the vulva, O you who bring all vulvas under control, O you whose form is the vulva, O eternally moist one, O you whose very nature is the vulva! Bring all vulvas to me! O bestower of boons, O you of excellent seed, O you of divine seed!
O you who are moist with the vulva, make them wet! Make them flow! O infallible one, O piercing vulva, agitate, cause all sentient beings to tremble!
Bhageśvarī aiṃ llūṃ jñeṃ vlūṃ peṃ llūṃ moṃ vlūṃ aiṃ klinne sarvāṇi bhagāni me vaśam ānaya svāhā strīṃ haraleṃ hrīṃ— this is the mantra of Bhagamālinī.
On the third day, having performed the morning bath and other rites as before, one should recite the *Nityaklinnā* mantra.
Having performed the salutation to the Guru and the *Mātṛkā-nyāsa*, [one should assign the mantras]: *hrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *nityā* to the head, *svāhā*;
*klinne* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *mada* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; and *drave* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
Svāhā! Astra! Phaṭ!
[I bow to her] who is ruddy, whose limbs are ruddy, who is as beautiful as the dawn, who wears a parrot, who is smeared with ruddy unguents, and whose lotus-face bears a lovely smile.
Her three eyes are wide open, her face is radiant with the pearls of perspiration on her forehead,
and she is adorned with a crown featuring a shimmering crescent moon as its crest;
she holds in her four hands a noose, a goad, and two vessels.
She bore the gesture of fearlessness, sat upon a lotus, and was languid with intoxication.

Having meditated thus, having bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as intended, one should again perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and practice the worship of Śrīvidyā. "Hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā" is the root mantra of Nityaklinnā.

On the fourth [lunar day], having performed the rites such as bathing at full moon, and having performed the salutation to the Guru and the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa), [one recites]: *krāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hraiṃ* to the head, *svāhā*;
*krauṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*).
*Hraum* to the armor, *huṃ*; *cchraum* to her endowed with three eyes; *jraum* to the weapon.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the two hands, [one should meditate on her] resembling molten gold, endowed with necklaces and three eyes.
Her face was graced with a beautiful smile, and she was adorned with divine ornaments.
Adorned with earrings, necklaces, armlets, and red garments,
she was exceedingly beautiful, graced by ornaments such as anklets and waves of ripples.
I worship her who holds a noose, a goad, a shield, a sword, a mace, fire, a bow, and arrows in her hands,
whether she is seated or otherwise positioned.

Having meditated thus, having bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as intended, one should again perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and practice the worship of Śrīvidyā. "Oṃ krauṃ hrauṃ krauṃ chrauṃ jrauṃ svāhā"—
this is the Bheruṇḍā mantra.

On the fifth day, having performed the bathing and other rites as before, and having performed the salutation to the Guru and the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkā-nyāsa), one performs the six-limbed ritual with *hrām* and so forth.
[She is] resembling molten gold, beautiful in her fresh youth.
Her lotus-face bears a beautiful smile, her three eyes are radiant,
and she is endowed with eight arms resplendent with rubies as ornaments;
she holds a red lotus, a *puṇḍra* sugarcane bow, a full-moon discus, and a sword.
Holding a *kalhāra* flower with a golden bee in her left arms,
and holding a citron (*mātuluṅga*) among flowers in her right hands,
she is surrounded on all sides by the *Śaktis* who are singing melodious notes.
Having meditated thus, having bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as intended,
one should again perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and then practice the worship of Śrīvidyā.
*Oṃ hrīṃ vahnivāsinyai namaḥ*— this is the mantra of Vahnivāsinī.
On the sixth [tithi], having bathed as before and performed the rites of bathing and so forth, one should mutter the Mahāvidyeśvarī mantra. (p.
44) Having performed the salutation to the Guru and the placement of the Mātṛkās (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*), [one recites]: *hrīṃ klīṃ neṃ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

*Hrīṃ aiṃ hlīṃ śrīṃ* on the head; *hrīṃ krauṃ hrīṃ* for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *hrīṃ nitya hrīṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*); *hrīṃ mada hrīṃ* for the eyes; *hlīṃ drave hrīṃ* for the weapon (*astra*).
[She is] red, clad in red garments, and adorned with red perfumes and garlands.
She has four arms and three eyes, and she is radiant with a crown of rubies.

Holding a noose, a goad, a staff, a sugarcane bow, and likewise a pomegranate as an arrow, she who is compassionate and cool with the intoxication [of bliss] should be meditated upon in this way; then, having bound the *yonimudrā*, one should perform the recitation as intended.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and further executed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā.
*Hrīṃ klinne aiṃ krauṃ nityamadadrave hrīṃ*: this is the mantra of Mahāvidyeśvarī.

On the seventh lunar day, having performed the morning bath and other rites as before, and having performed the salutation to the Guru and the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual with *hrāḥ* and so forth [to the respective limbs]. [She is] equal in luster to the midday sun during the summer season.
She wears a crown of nine jewels, has three eyes, and is clad in crimson garments;
she is endowed with nine ornaments and her bodily luster is radiant.
With a pure smile and eight arms, she is being praised by the great sages.
She holds a noose, a shield, and a chisel, as well as a cup, with her left arms;
likewise, with her right hands, she holds a goad, a sword, an axe, and a lotus.
Having meditated thus upon her who is endowed with the effort to grant the desires of the practitioner, and having performed the recitation as intended while forming the *yonimudrā*,
one should offer it and perform the worship of Śrīvidyā: *hrīṃ śivadūtyai namaḥ*.
Thus ends the Śivadūtī mantra.
On the eighth lunar day, having performed the ritual bathing and other rites as before, and having performed the salutation to the Guru and the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, [one recites]:
*sve* for the heart, *ca* for the head, *che* for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *chekṣā* with *vaṣaṭ*, and *kṣastrīṃ*.
*Kavacāya* (for the armor): *strīṃ haṃ*. *Netratrayāya* (for the three eyes): *haṃ*. *Khakṣeṃ astrāya phaṭ* (for the weapon: *phaṭ*). Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the hands and limbs.
Dark-complexioned, performing auspicious deeds, and radiant with fresh youth;
resplendent with ornaments fashioned from eight parts arranged in groups of two and three;
likewise adorned with earrings, armlets, a girdle, and anklets.
She possesses a formidable form composed of the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras;
she is clothed in cowherd garments,
her arms are adorned with beautiful moving peacock-feather ornaments, and she is radiant with a crown of rubies.
She has a crest made of peacock feathers, with those very feathers as her banners;
her chest and breasts are adorned with strings of *guñjā* berries, and she is decorated with saffron.
She possesses three eyes and a beautiful face, her lotus-like countenance graced by a gentle smile.
She has four radiant arms, holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.

Having meditated thus, having bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as intended, one should offer it and perform the worship of Śrīvidyā. *Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ khe ca che kṣa strīṃ haṃ kṣeṃ hīṃ phaṭ*—this is Tvaritā. Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), [one should proceed].
She is red, attended by a multitude of red-bodied Śaktis;
she is red, adorned with parrots, garlands, and unguents, and possesses six lotus-faces.
Each face has three eyes, and her countenance is graced with a beautiful smile.

Having meditated thus upon her who is radiant with a crown of rubies set with priceless gems, and having formed the *yonimudrā*, performed the intended recitation (*japa*), and offered it, one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā. *Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*— this is the *Kulasundarī* mantra.
On the tenth day, having performed the morning bath and other rites, having paid homage to the Guru, having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*,
and having performed the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual with the syllable *Hrāṃ*—
[one should meditate on the Goddess] who resembles the rising sun and is radiant with a crown of rubies.
Adorned with ornaments made of rubies and wearing crimson garments, she was [beheld].
46) Due to negligence, the text here has been omitted.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] who shines with the lotus-face of a beautiful, radiant smile,
and having formed the *yonimudrā*, one should perform the recitation as intended.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and offered [them], one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā.
"Hasakalaraḍaiṃ hasakalaraṇḍī hasakalaraḍauḥ" is the Nityā mantra.
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), having performed the morning bath and other rites, and having performed the salutation to the Guru and the Mātṛkā-nyāsa,
[one recites]: *hrīṃ phreṃ* for the heart, *sktaṃ kroṃ* for the head with *svāhā*, *āṃ klīṃ* for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) with *vaṣaṭ*,
*aiṃ vlūṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*) with *hum*, and *nityamadadrave* for the three eyes, followed by *kṣeṃ preṃ hrīṃ* for the weapon (*astra*).

Having thus meditated upon her— who resembles a sapphire, is adorned with a crown of radiant jewels, possesses five faces and three eyes, and wears crimson garments— and having formed the *yonimudrā*, performed the prescribed recitation (*japa*), and offered it;
One should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā.
*Hrīṃ phreṃ sruṃ kroṃ āṃ klīṃ aiṃ vlūṃ nityamadadrave huṃ pheṃ hīṃ*— this is the mantra of Nīlapatākā.
On the twelfth day, having performed the morning bath and other rites, and having performed the salutation to the Guru and the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should perform the *maṅga-nyāsa* as follows:
*bhāṃ* to the heart, *bhe* to the head, *ī* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *kṣeṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *yaiṃ* to the three eyes, and *oṃ* to the two arms (*bāhu*).
This is the *maṅga-nyāsa*.
She has five faces and ten arms, with three eyes in each face;
she is resplendent with a radiant crown adorned by a crescent moon.
With her left arms, she holds a conch, a shield, two nooses, and a white lotus.
Holding a discus, a goad, a sword, an arrow,
and a citron in her right hands, gentle and seated in a comfortable posture—
having meditated thus, having bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation as intended, one should offer it to Śrī.
One should perform the worship of the Vidyā:
*hrīṃ phreṃ sruṃ kroṃ āṃ klīṃ aiṃ vlūṃ nityamadadrave huṃ pheṃ hāṃ*. (p. 48)
The mantra of Nīlapatākā is *bhamaraya*. The mantra of Vijayā is *oṃ oṃ*.

On the thirteenth day, having performed the morning bath and other rites, having paid homage to the Guru and performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, [he who is] endowed with the six limbs including the *sāmidhenī* [mantras],
[should meditate on her] as golden-hued, beautiful, and adorned with pearls and rubies.
She wears a crown of rubies, with two eyes that are slightly trembling;
she has two arms and sits upon her own seat, a lotus, amidst sixteen petals and their twice-eight [thirty-two] sub-petals. She resides within a temple of eyebrows possessing four doors.
Holding a *nātuliṅga* fruit in her right lotus-hand,
she bestows curd and other offerings with her left hand upon her own devotees;
she is surrounded on all sides by Śaktis who are equal to herself.

Having meditated thus and bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) as intended, one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā for the attainment of all goals. "Svauḥ" is the mantra of Sarvamaṅgalā.
On the fourteenth day, having performed the morning bath and other rites, one should perform the salutation to the Guru and the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.

Having performed [the nyāsa]: Oṃ, salutation to the heart; Svāhā to the head; O Bhagavatī, Jvālāmālinī, to the crest-lock; Huṃ to the armor; O Goddess, destroyer of all beings, to the three eyes; [and] the weapon-mantra: [I meditate upon her] who resembles a blazing fire, radiant with a crown of rubies.
She has six faces and twelve arms, adorned with all ornaments;
she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose and a goad, a sword and a shield,
a bow and arrows, a mace, a trident, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus upon her being surrounded on all sides by her own equal Śaktis, and having formed the Yonimudrā, performed the recitation as intended, and offered it,
one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Goddess Jvālāmālinī, you who effect the destruction of all beings, O Jātavedas!
Blaze, blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ! Ra ra ra ra ra ra ra ra! O Jvālāmālinī, hūṃ phaṭ!
*Svāhā*. This is the mantra of Jvālāmālinī.

On the fifteenth day of both lunar fortnights, having performed the morning bath and other rites, having paid homage to the Guru and performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, and having performed the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual beginning with *cām*—
Resembling the orb of the rising sun, adorned with the nine precious gems,
wearing a crown of the nine jewels and soft garments of variegated silk;
four-armed, three-eyed, with a face radiant with a pure smile.

Consisting entirely of bliss, eternal, bestowing all auspiciousness— four-armed, holding in her hands the noose, the goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness; the auspicious Padmā, who dwells within the fresh source at the center of the lotus.
Having meditated thus, having bound the *yonimudrā*, and having performed the recitation as intended and offered it,
one should perform the worship of Śrīvidyā.

"Ktvauṃ" is the root mantra of Citrā. However, according to the Kādimata, there is a rule that one should perform the worship of the respective Nityās on their corresponding lunar days (tithis), proceeding in order from Kāmeśvarī to Citrā, starting from the first day of both the bright and dark fortnights up to the fifteenth day. Therefore, [the following] are the nyāsa, mantras, and meditations for them.
[The mantras] have been written down. Since the fifteen Nityās are portions of the Supreme Deity (paradevatā), their seer (ṛṣi) and meter (chandas) are those of the Root Deity.

For example, as Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, and Kāmeśvarī Nityā is the deity, so one should act accordingly; that is, one should act according to each respective name—this is the sequence of instruction.
Thus ends the sequence for daily worship in the *Cinmantramālinī*, composed by the venerable Prakāśānanda.
Samvat 1719, [the year of] Rāma.
